In [[computability theory]], there are a number of '''basis theorems'''. These theorems show that particular kinds of sets always must have some members that are, in terms of [[Turing degree]], not too complicated. One family of basis theorems concern nonempty effectively closed sets (that is, nonempty <math>\Pi^0_1</math> sets in the [[arithmetical hierarchy]]); these theorems are studied as part of classical computability theory. Another family of basis theorems concern nonempty lightface [[analytic set]]s (that is, <math>\Sigma^1_1</math> in the [[analytical hierarchy]]); these theorems are studied as part of [[hyperarithmetical theory]].

== Effectively closed sets ==

Effectively closed sets are a topic of study in classical computability theory. An effectively closed set is the set of all paths through some computable [[Tree (descriptive set theory)|subtree]] of the binary tree <math>2^{<\omega}</math>. These sets are closed, [[closed set|in the topological sense]], as subsets of the [[Cantor space]] <math>2^\omega</math>, and the complement of an effective closed set is an effective open set in the sense of [[effective Polish space]]s. [[Stephen Cole Kleene|Kleene]] proved in 1952 that there is a nonempty, effectively closed set with no computable point (Cooper 1999, p.&nbsp;134). Basis theorems show that there must be points that are not "too far" from being computable, in an informal sense.

A class <math>\mathcal{C} \subseteq 2^\omega</math> is a '''basis''' for effectively closed sets if every nonempty effectively closed set includes a member of&nbsp;<math>\mathcal{C}</math> (Cooper&nbsp;2003, p.&nbsp;329). Basis theorems show that particular classes are bases in this sense. These theorems include (Cooper 1999, p.&nbsp;134): 
* The '''[[low basis theorem]]''': each nonempty <math>\Pi^0_1</math> set has a member that is of low degree. 
* The '''hyperimmune-free basis theorem''': each nonempty <math>\Pi^0_1</math> set has a member that is of [[hyperimmune-free]] degree. 
* The '''r.e. basis theorem''': each nonempty <math>\Pi^0_1</math> set has a member that is of [[Recursively enumerable Turing degree|recursively enumerable (r.e.) degree]].

Here, a set <math>X \subseteq \N</math> is ''low'' if its [[Turing jump]] <math>X' = \varnothing'</math>, the degree of the [[halting problem]]. <math>X</math> has ''hyperimmune-free degree'' if every total <math>X</math>-computable function <math>f\colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}</math> is dominated by a total computable function <math>g</math> (meaning <math>f(n) \leq g(n)</math> for all <math>n</math>).

No two of the above three theorems can be combined for the set of consistent completions of [[Peano arithmetic|PA]] (or just [[Exponential function arithmetic|EFA]]; the Turing degrees are the same).  The only r.e. Turing degree that computes a consistent completion of PA is 0'.  However, the low basis theorem and the hyperimmune-free basis theorem can each be combined with cone avoidance, i.e. for every noncomputable ''X'', we can choose a member (as in the theorem) that does not compute ''X''.  The theorems also relativize above an arbitrary real.

== Lightface analytic sets ==

There are also basis theorems for lightface <math>\Sigma^1_1</math> sets. These basis theorems are studied as part of [[hyperarithmetical theory]]. One theorem is the Gandy basis theorem, which is analogous to the low basis theorem. The '''Gandy basis theorem''' shows that each nonempty <math>\Sigma^1_1</math> set has an element that is hyperarithmetically low, that is its hyperjump has the same hyperdegree (and for the theorem, even the same Turing degree) as [[Kleene's O|Kleene's set <math>\mathcal{O}</math>]].
